newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Generale shares jump on SNCF deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Generale shares jump on SNCF deal.

text.p: Shares in Generale des Eaux hit an all-time high on Thursday after its Cegetel telecoms unit was selected to run a network owned by the SNCF railroads, boosting its position as a rival to France Telecom.

The state-owned rail group Societe Nationale des Chemins de Fer (SNCF) said on Wednesday evening it had selected Cegetel over Bouygues Telecom to become its industrial partner in its Telecom Developpement unit.
Generale closed 26 francs ($4.57), or 3.35 percent higher, at 802 francs, while Bouygues shares plunged 30 francs, or 5.15 percent, to 553 francs.

Cegetel will have a 49.9 percent stake under a deal to be finalised before March 31. The pact gives Cegetel access to the SNCF network of 8,000 kilometres of optic fibre all over the country, as well as radio links, which will be expanded to some 12,000 kilometres in the next six years.
The deal will bost its effort to become the main rival of France Telecom when the market is fully liberalised in 1998 and will also generate savings in infrastructure investments.
"The operator that has the SNCF network is clearly going to be the number two in France (after France Telecom)," an analyst at a French brokerage said.
Generale des Eaux is the controlling shareholder in Cegetel and has British Telecom Plc, Germany's Mannesmann AG and SBC Communications Inc of the United States as partners.
Cegetel already runs France's second-biggest mobile telecommunications network SFR, which on Thursday said it had more than one million subscribers.

Generale des Eaux chairman Jean-Marie Messier has said that Cegetel aims to have 20 percent of the French fixed-line telephone market within five years and 10 percent for business services. Cegetel is already trying out a fixed-line service in the Mediterranean city of Nice.
It also has experience using television cable networks for telecommunications through a British unit in Windsor.
In France, however, the company will not use the television cable solution but instead concentrate on a new technology called DECT -- digitally-enhanced cordless telephone.

Generale des Eaux last week concluded a deal in which it took a bigger stake in media group Havas after transferring its stake in television company Canal Plus to Havas. It will sell its cable networks.
The deal will allow Cegetel to offer value-added services such as Internet access and on-line services as well as the more traditional telecommunications services.

At Bouygues, meanwhile, a spokeswoman said the company still aimed to become a full telecommunications operator and was on the look-out for other existing networks, such as those owned by state utility Electricite de France or by toll roads.

Bouygues counts Germany's VEBA and Italy's STET among its partners, and industry analysts said they did not exclude a further tie-up with AT & T and Unisource -- a consortium made up of Dutch KPN, Telia AB of Sweden, Swiss Telecom PTT and Spain's Telefonica.
"Bouygues will end up in the arms of AT&T," an analyst said. ($ = 5.687 French Francs)
